title: Staining a Few Neurons to See Them Whole
endLine: Stain a few cells completely to see shape, not gaps or motion.

scenes.tts: How do you trace one neuron inside a tangled slice of brain? Stain every cell, and you get a dense crowd of bodies wrapped in threads. No eye can follow a single branch from start to end. In 1873, a surprising stain turned that puzzle around.
scenes.caption: How do you trace one neuron inside a tangled slice of brain? Stain every cell, and you get a dense crowd of bodies wrapped in threads. No eye can follow a single branch from start to end. In 1873, a surprising stain turned that puzzle around.
scenes.visual: Full-frame cross-section of a slice of brain tissue under a light microscope (schematic), filling over 60% of frame height. Every cell body and branching thread darkens into a dense, overlapping tangle while a slow focus drift moves across the slice. A bright tracer tries to follow one thread and loses it in the crowd. Label '1873' appears cleanly at the end.
scenes.narration: How do you trace one neuron inside a tangled slice of brain? Stain every cell, and you get a dense crowd of bodies wrapped in threads. No eye can follow a single branch from start to end. In 1873, a surprising stain turned that puzzle around.

scenes.visual: The tangled brain slice dims softly while its threads keep a slow ambient drift (schematic). High-contrast title 'Staining a Few Neurons to See Them Whole' appears centred over the slice for 2 seconds, then fades as the slice clears.

scenes.tts: A Nissl stain binds R N A rich cytoplasm around every nucleus, marking cell bodies and layer boundaries. Golgi's silver chromate stain does the opposite. For reasons nobody fully understands, it blackens only a small, unpredictable fraction of cells. Yet each stained neuron fills almost completely, revealing every dendrite and fibre against a clear background.

scenes.visual: Same brain slice (schematic, no molecular structures). First, a Nissl-stain sweep lights up cytoplasm around every nucleus, outlining rows of cell bodies and layer borders while fine branches stay faint. Next, the slice clears and silver chromate washes across: almost every cell stays transparent while three scattered neurons slowly turn jet black from cell body out to every dendrite and nerve fibre against a clear background.

scenes.tts: Seeing whole neurons sharpened an old question. Is the nervous system separate cells, like liver or skin, or one continuous network of fused fibres? Zoom into this same stained slice where two blackened branches meet. Can Golgi's stain under a light microscope prove whether those two cells are separate or fused?

scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly into the same Golgi-stained slice (schematic) until two jet-black branches approach and touch at the centre of the frame. Brief schematic callouts contrast separate cells versus fused fibres, then fade as the contact point zooms large and the high-contrast question 'Separate cells, or fused fibres?' appears.

scenes.visual: Hold on the zoomed junction of the two blackened branches inside the stained slice (schematic) with the question 'Separate cells, or fused fibres?' on screen. A subtle focus ring breathes gently around the meeting point while a slim 4.5-second timer bar fills smoothly along the bottom.

scenes.tts: No. Light blurs tiny gaps. The best light microscope blurs points closer than about two hundred nanometres side to side. At a chemical synapse, where one cell signals the next, the gap is about twenty nanometres. Two hundred divided by twenty is ten, so the gap sits ten times below the limit. Where branches met, Golgi and Cajal saw no gap.

scenes.visual: At the zoomed junction in the same slice, an optical blur disc computed to scale expands to 200 nm across, engulfing the junction. Inside that disc, a computed to-scale 20 nm chemical synapse gap appears ten times narrower while '200 nm / 20 nm = 10x' builds on screen as each number is spoken. The blur then closes back over the gap so the two branches look merged.

scenes.tts: Two more limits hide in the same slice. A stained section is one hundred micrometres or more thick. Focusing up and down blurs roughly zero point five to one micrometre, so stacked branches look joined. Every Golgi specimen is also dead, fixed tissue. A still picture shows shape and position, never movement and never a cell's descendants.

scenes.visual: The same slice tilts slightly to show its 100-micrometre-or-more thickness (schematic). A focus plane sweeps up and down with a blurred 0.5 to 1 micrometre band, making two separated branches at different depths appear to cross and fuse. Then the frame locks into a still image of short, medium, and long fibres to show that fixed tissue reveals shape and position, not movement or descendants.

scenes.tts: Experimenters guard against these traps by pairing methods. Because Golgi fills an unpredictable fraction, Nissl stains handle cell counts and layer boundaries. Immunostaining uses an antibody against one chosen protein to test whether that target was detected. Electron microscopy resolves true gaps, while proving movement takes more than extra fixed sections.

scenes.visual: Same brain slice stays anchored in frame while three companion overlays sweep across it one by one (all schematic, no molecular structures): first a Nissl overlay lights up every cell body to count layers; next an antibody-detection glow marks cells where one target protein is detected; finally an electron-microscope inset zooms sharply into the junction to reveal a clean gap, while stacked still frames fade beside moving markers to show fixed sections cannot prove motion.

scenes.tts: Used within those limits, Golgi's stain unlocked foundational discoveries. Its 1873 arrival let Golgi and Cajal argue separate cells versus fused fibres with evidence. In 1890, Santiago Ramón y Cajal stained chick embryo spinal cords a few days old. He found young nerve fibres ending in a swollen club with spikes, and named it the growth cone.

scenes.visual: Same microscope-slice world shifts smoothly between two historical views (schematic). First, labelled '1873', blackened individual neurons stand cleanly isolated in the slice as separate-cells versus fused-fibres lines appear. Next, labelled '1890: Growth cone', the slice shifts to chick embryo spinal cord: young black nerve fibres of different lengths appear, zooming onto one tip that forms a swollen club with spikes and fine projections.

scenes.tts: In 1972, Pasko Rakic paired Golgi stains with serial electron microscopy in fetal rhesus monkey cortex. He found young neurons pressed against radial fibres on their way to the cortical plate. Pairing methods answered what light alone could not. Leaving most cells unseen reveals whole shapes, once paired with tools for gaps and motion.

scenes.visual: Same microscope-slice world morphs to fetal rhesus monkey cortex, labelled '1972' (schematic): tall radial fibres span the slice toward the cortical plate at top, with blackened young neurons pressed tightly against them while a crisp electron-microscope inset confirms their close contact. The view then pulls back to the original clear slice holding a single complete black neuron drifting slowly in focus.
